name: Anaconda, Inc.
subcategory: Python/R data-science distribution and package repository; enterprise AI platform
origin_detail: Founded 2012 in Austin, Texas, as Continuum Analytics by Travis Oliphant (creator of NumPy, SciPy contributor) and Peter Wang, out of the scientific-Python community; early DARPA funding (2013); renamed Anaconda in 2017
openness_notes: The underlying tools (conda, Numba, Bokeh and the packaged libraries) are OSI-licensed, but the distribution itself is 'freemium': the individual edition is freeware and the curated repository is governed by terms of service. Since 2020 organizations with 200+ employees must buy a commercial licence to use Anaconda's repository, and by 2023-2024 the academic/non-profit exemption was dropped (teaching use still exempt). Enterprise tiers are proprietary SaaS. Level 2 throughout, with a clear restricting trend.

license_history.license: OSI-licensed tools (conda BSD-3, Numba, Bokeh) plus free Anaconda distribution
Terms of service: fee for 'heavy commercial use' of the repository (Apr 2020), defined as orgs with >200 employees (Oct 2020)
license_history.note: Packages keep their own licences; the restriction is on Anaconda's repository/service

license_history.license: Terms of service (Mar 2024): government and non-profit entities with >200 employees or contractors must pay; teaching exempt
license_history.note: Academic/non-profit exclusion had been dropped by May 2023 without apparent notice

relicensing_events.to: Paid commercial licence required for organizations >200 people (extended to non-profits/academia by 2023-2024)
relicensing_events.fork: conda-forge (community channel) and Miniforge are the usual alternatives
relicensing_events.fork_backer: Community (conda-forge); not verified in fetched pages
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Not an OSI licence change but a terms-of-service paywall. In 2024 Anaconda sent legal demands to academic and non-profit institutions threatening back-billing; Mass General Brigham removed Anaconda from its HPC cluster's general repositories

risk_events: 2020-2024 terms-of-service changes turned a de facto free scientific tool into a licensed product for large organizations, including universities and non-profits
2024: legal demands to academic institutions threatening back-billing; HPC sites removed Anaconda from shared repositories
Aug 2024: Anaconda sued Intel for copyright infringement over use of its software on an expired licence
Leadership turnover: CEO Barry Libert replaced by David DeSanto (ex-GitLab CPO) in Oct 2025; new CFO Aug 2026
2026 pivot to enterprise AI via three acquisitions in four months (Outerbounds Apr 2026, Kilo Code Jul 2026, Enkrypt AI Aug 2026)
robustness: The tools Anaconda popularized are robust independently of the company: conda is open source and the community-run conda-forge channel and Miniforge installer provide a licence-free path. The company itself is mid-sized (~300 staff in 2024) and VC-funded at a $1.5B valuation, with heavy user reach (40-50M users; 1.2M organizations) but low conversion of that reach into revenue (revenue undisclosed).
physical_science_relevance: Very high: Anaconda/conda is a default way to install the scientific Python stack on lab machines and HPC clusters; its 2020-2024 licensing changes directly forced universities and research hospitals to audit, pay or migrate to conda-forge.
openness_effect_assessment: Free distribution of open scientific Python made Anaconda ubiquitous (2M users in 2015 to 40-50M by 2024-2026) but left little to sell; the company responded by gating its repository service behind a commercial licence and then enforcing it against academia. That generated revenue pressure on institutions and reputational damage, while the community-run conda-forge provided an exit, limiting Anaconda's leverage.
key_takeaway: Anaconda is a cautionary case for scientific software: a company built on community open-source (NumPy/SciPy lineage) monetized by restricting access to the convenience layer (repository and installer) rather than the code, which shifted costs onto universities. Its 2025 raise at $1.5B and 2026 AI acquisitions show investors now value it as an enterprise AI platform rather than as a science tool.
